title: Making features
objectives: Build interaction and polynomial features, and see when they overfit.
Encode sectors as dummies and reject features not known at prediction time.

screens.title: One slope is not enough
screens.prose: Eight shares: four volatile ($\text{vol} = +1$) and four calm ($\text{vol} = -1$). The model is $\hat y = 0.3 + 0.7\,\text{mom} - 0.2\,\text{vol} + b_3\,(\text{mom} \times \text{vol})$. With $b_3 = 0$ both groups get the same slope.

derive.caption: Slope for volatile shares {{fixed(0.7 + b3, 2)}}, for calm shares {{fixed(0.7 - b3, 2)}}

screens.question: Set $b_3$ so each line runs through its own four shares.

hints.text: The volatile shares rise steeply; the calm ones barely move.
The volatile shares climb 1.2% per unit of mom. Their slope is $0.7 + b_3$.
$0.7 + b_3 = 1.2$ gives $b_3 = 0.5$. Check the calm slope: $0.7 - 0.5 = 0.2$.

feedback.correct: With $b_3 = 0.5$ momentum earns 1.2 per unit in volatile shares and 0.2 in calm ones.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption: the volatile slope should be 1.2 and the calm slope 0.2.

byKey.flat: With $b_3$ near 0 both groups share one slope, so the line misses both groups.
byKey.neg: You tilted the wrong way. A negative $b_3$ makes momentum pay more in calm shares.

explain.text: You found $b_3 = 0.5$: the slope on mom is $0.7 + 0.5\,\text{vol}$, so it depends on vol. A model with mom and vol alone cannot do that. The extra column $\text{mom} \times \text{vol}$ lets one feature change the effect of another.

screens.title: Building the column
screens.prose: The column you just used is an **interaction**: the product of two features, row by row. It is a new feature like any other, and OLS fits its coefficient as usual. Build it for four shares.

derive.caption: Slope for volatile shares {{fixed(0.7 + b3, 2)}}, for calm shares {{fixed(0.7 - b3, 2)}}

screens.question: Fill in $\text{mom} \times \text{vol}$ for each share.

hints.text: Multiply the two numbers in each row.
Watch the signs: two negatives make a positive.

feedback.correct: Share D, a loser among volatile-looking shares, gets the largest value: 3.0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply mom by vol in each row and keep the sign.

explain.text: The products are 0.6, −1.2, −0.4 and 3.0. Share D has negative mom and negative vol, yet its interaction is positive. That is why an interaction is read through its slope, $0.7 + b_3\,\text{vol}$, not on its own.

screens.title: Every pair at once
screens.prose: A desk wants every pairwise interaction of its features appended to $\mathbf{X}$. These are columns $x_ix_j$ for each pair $i < j$, in the order $(0, 1), (0, 2), \dots, (1, 2), \dots$.
screens.question: Complete `add_interactions(X)` so it returns $\mathbf{X}$ with every pairwise product appended.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: the arrays are compared with math.isclose entry by entry, and one test checks the shape. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Column $i$ of `X` is `X[:, i]`.
Each new column is a row-by-row product of two columns.
`X[:, i] * X[:, j]` inside the list.

feedback.correct: Four features gain six products: 10 columns.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Each new column is `X[:, i] * X[:, j]` for one pair $i < j$.

explain.text: `combinations` lists each pair once with $i < j$, so $p$ features gain $p(p-1)/2$ products. A single column has no pairs and comes back unchanged. A feature paired with itself would be its square, which `combinations` skips.

screens.title: Polynomial features
screens.prose: `PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)` goes further: every product of up to two features, squares included. Two features $x_0, x_1$ become five columns. The square $x_0^2$ is the interaction of $x_0$ with itself.
screens.question: How many columns does `PolynomialFeatures` make?

hints.text: For degree 2: the features, their squares, then the products of two different features.
Five features: 5 linear, 5 squares and $\binom{5}{2} = 10$ products.
Degree 2: $5 + 5 + 10 = 20$. Degree 3 adds the 35 products of three: 55. Ten features at degree 2: $10 + 10 + 45 = 65$.

feedback.correct: 20, 55 and 65: the columns grow far faster than the features.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count linear terms, squares and cross products separately.

explain.text: Five features make 20 columns at degree 2 and 55 at degree 3. In general there are $\binom{p + d}{d} - 1$ columns. Each one is a coefficient to estimate from the same rows.

screens.title: Counting degree 2
screens.prose: Why does degree 2 give $p(p + 3)/2$ columns? Put the count in order.
screens.question: Put the lines of the count in order.

lines.text: Degree 2, a feature times itself: $p$ squares $x_j^2$
Degree 2, two different features: $\binom{p}{2} = p(p - 1)/2$ products $x_ix_j$ with $i < j$
Total: $p + p + p(p - 1)/2 = p(p + 3)/2$, which is 20 for $p = 5$

hints.text: Every column has degree 1 or degree 2.
A degree-2 column multiplies either one feature by itself or two different features.
List the three kinds of column, then add them: $2p + p(p - 1)/2$.

feedback.correct: Three kinds of column, then the sum.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The sum comes last, after the three kinds of column.

byKey.sum: The total needs all three counts first.

explain.text: $2p + \tfrac{p(p-1)}{2} = \tfrac{4p + p^2 - p}{2} = \tfrac{p(p + 3)}{2}$. For $p = 10$ that is 65, and the square term makes it grow like $p^2$.

You followed the training line. Degree 3 fits training rows better but tests at 3.12.

The test line has one low point.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the lowest point of the test line.

screens.title: Polynomial fit in code
screens.prose: Wrap the expansion and the fit together. Learn the transform on the training rows with `fit_transform`, then apply it to the test rows with `transform`. `make_curved(seed, n)` builds panels like the chart's.
screens.question: Complete `poly_test_mse` so it returns the test MSE of OLS on polynomial features, rounded to 6 places.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np

def make_curved(seed, n=400):
    """Three features (mom, vol, value) as z-scores, rows in month order.
    Momentum pays more in volatile shares: the true model has a mom x vol term."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    X = rng.standard_normal((n, 3))
    y = 0.3 + 0.5 * X[:, 0] - 0.3 * X[:, 1] + 0.6 * X[:, 0] * X[:, 1] + 1.5 * rng.standard_normal(n)
    return X, y

widget.solution:
from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import mean_squared_error

def poly_test_mse(X_train, y_train, X_test, y_test, degree):
    pf = PolynomialFeatures(degree=degree, include_bias=False)
    P_train = pf.fit_transform(X_train)
    P_test = pf.transform(X_test)
    model = LinearRegression().fit(P_train, y_train)
    return round(float(mean_squared_error(y_test, model.predict(P_test))), 6)
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on panels from `make_curved(seed, n)`, which is already defined, at degrees 1 to 4. Each MSE is compared with math.isclose. The first run loads scikit-learn and NumPy, which takes 10 to 30 seconds; later runs are quick.

hints.text: `fit_transform` learns and applies in one call; `transform` only applies.
Call `fit_transform` on `X_train` and `transform` on `X_test`.
`P_train = pf.fit_transform(X_train)` and `P_test = pf.transform(X_test)`.

feedback.correct: On `make_curved(1)` degree 2 tests at 2.4135, against 2.6938 for degree 1.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Expand both sets with the same `pf`, learned on the training rows.

explain.text: On panel 1 the test MSE runs 2.694, 2.413 and 2.633 for degrees 1 to 3. `PolynomialFeatures` learns nothing from the values, only the column count. A scaler does learn from values, which is why we keep the fit-on-train habit from now on.

screens.title: Sectors as columns
screens.prose: A sector is text, so give each sector a 0 or 1 column: a **dummy**. With an intercept, drop the first sector's column. Otherwise the dummies add up to the column of ones, and $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular.

state.caption: Sorted sectors: Banks, Energy, Tech. Banks is dropped: it is the base the intercept stands for.

screens.question: Complete `one_hot(sectors)`: sort the unique sectors, drop the first, and return one 0/1 column per remaining sector.

widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests: three compare the 0/1 matrix exactly, one its shape and one its total. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Each row has a 1 in its own sector's column, if that column was kept.
Banks rows are all zeros: the dropped base.
`1 if s == lev else 0` inside the inner list.

feedback.correct: Base-sector rows are all zeros; every other row has one 1.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Put a 1 where the share's sector matches the column's sector, else 0.

explain.text: Each kept column's coefficient is that sector's average gap from Banks, the base. With all three columns plus the intercept, Banks = $1 - \text{Energy} - \text{Tech}$, so no unique fit exists. One sector only gives zero columns: there is nothing to compare it with.

screens.title: Too good to be true
screens.prose: We predict February's return for 400 share-months, from data as of 31 January. A colleague tests five features one at a time on held-out months. One result is astonishing.
screens.question: Tap the feature the desk must remove before anything else.

hints.text: Read the second column. When would each value be known?
Prediction happens on 31 January. One feature is not known until 28 February.
February's buying volume happens during the month being predicted. It is part of the answer, not a clue to it.

feedback.correct: February's buying volume is not known on 31 January. It leaks the target.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check when each feature becomes known.

byKey.r2: You dropped the weakest feature. A weak test $R^2$ is normal for returns; the astonishing one is the problem.
byKey.r0: Past-month return is known on 31 January. Its small score is what real signals look like.
byKey.r1: Volatility over the past 60 days is known on 31 January. Its score is plausible.
byKey.r3: Market cap on 31 January is known in time. Its score is small and plausible.

explain.text: Buying volume in February moves with February's return, so it scores 44.92%. It does that by containing the answer: it is **leakage**. Any feature that is not known when the forecast is made has to go, however good it looks.

screens.title: The feature rules
screens.prose: New features are functions of old ones: products, powers, logs, lags and dummies. Degree $d$ on $p$ features gives $$\binom{p + d}{d} - 1 \text{ columns},$$ so test error, not training error, decides how far to go. Every feature must be computable at prediction time, and any transform is learned on training rows only.
screens.question: Four features at degree 3: how many columns does `PolynomialFeatures(include_bias=False)` make?

options.why: You kept the constant column. `include_bias=False` drops it: $\binom{7}{3} - 1 = 34$.
You counted ordered triples, $4^3$. The product $x_0x_1x_2$ is one column, not six.
You counted each feature to powers 1, 2 and 3 only. The cross products count too.

hints.text: Use $\binom{p + d}{d} - 1$ with $p = 4$ and $d = 3$.

feedback.correct: $\binom{7}{3} - 1 = 34$, matching the chart's degree-4 count for three features.

explain.text: $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ monomials of degree at most 3, minus the constant: 34. The counts in the chart, 3, 9, 19 and 34, come from the same formula with $p = 3$.

screens.title: Point in time
screens.prose: The desk adds $\text{mom} \times \text{vol}$ as a live feature: momentum has paid more in volatile shares. Its rule: a feature is allowed only if it could be computed at the close on 30 April. That is when May's forecast is made.

rows: Price and shares at the 30 April close

screens.question: Select all that apply: which features pass the rule?

options.why: You used the corrected number. On 30 April only the original filing existed; a database that overwrites history leaks June into April.
You used an announcement from inside May. It is part of what the forecast is trying to anticipate.

options.text: Log market cap at the 30 April close

hints.text: For each source, ask: did it exist on 30 April?
Two sources are dated after 30 April.
Keep mom × vol, sectors, the April filing and the April market cap. Drop the June restatement and the May results.

feedback.correct: Four pass; the June restatement and the May earnings fail.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep exactly the features whose data existed on 30 April.

byKey.rest: The restated value did not exist on 30 April. Point-in-time data keeps what was known then.
byKey.earn: Results on 15 May fall inside the month being predicted.

explain.text: **Point-in-time** data stores each value as it was known on each date. A restated book value is the subtle leak: the number is about the past, but it was published later. Interactions and logs are fine as long as their ingredients pass the rule.

ideas: An interaction $x_ix_j$ lets one feature change another's slope; a square is a feature's interaction with itself.
Polynomial features multiply quickly, $\binom{p+d}{d} - 1$ columns, and test error decides the degree.
Dummies drop one level beside an intercept, and every feature must be known when the forecast is made.

quiz.prose: A model has an intercept and a dummy for every one of its 11 sectors, none dropped.
quiz.question: What goes wrong?

options.text: The dummies add up to the ones column, so the coefficients are not unique
Nothing: more dummies give a more detailed model
options.why: You added the base sector back. Its column equals 1 minus the others, so OLS cannot separate it from the intercept.

options.text: It overfits, but the coefficients are still unique
options.why: It is worse than overfitting: with exact collinearity infinitely many coefficient sets give the same fit.
Nothing forces that. You could drop the intercept yourself, but OLS will not choose for you.

feedback.correct: Perfect collinearity: one column is an exact sum of others.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add up the 11 dummy columns on any row.

explain.text: Every share is in exactly one sector, so the 11 dummies sum to 1 on every row: the intercept's column. $\mathbf{X}^T\mathbf{X}$ is singular. Drop one sector, which then becomes the base.

quiz.prose: One sector, Shipping, has a single share in the training rows. Its dummy is kept.
quiz.question: What does the fitted model do with that share?

options.text: Fits its training return exactly: its dummy absorbs whatever the other features miss
Gives it the average sector effect
options.why: You expected pooling. A dummy's coefficient is free, and with one share it simply matches that share.

options.text: Drops the dummy because it is too rare
options.why: OLS never drops a column on its own.
Only a column of zeros gets 0. This one is 1 on the Shipping row.

feedback.correct: A one-share dummy is a private intercept for that share: pure noise for forecasting.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The dummy is 1 on exactly one row.

explain.text: The coefficient can move that one prediction anywhere without touching other rows, so OLS sets its residual to 0. The Shipping effect is then one share's one return: noise. Merge tiny sectors into a broader one.

byKey.bias: You kept the constant; `include_bias=False` drops it.
byKey.pow: You counted only powers of single features. Cross products such as $x_0x_1x_2$ count too.
byKey.cube: You counted ordered triples. Order does not matter in a product.

explain.text: $\binom{6}{3} = 20$ monomials of degree at most 3, minus the constant: 19.

quiz.prose: A colleague calls `.fit` on two transforms using all 400 rows, test rows included. They are `PolynomialFeatures` and `StandardScaler`, which subtracts each column's mean.
quiz.question: Which one leaks information from the test rows?

options.text: Only the scaler: it learns means from the data; the polynomial expansion learns nothing but a column count

options.why: `PolynomialFeatures` computes each row from that row alone, so the test rows change nothing. The habit of fitting on train is still right.

options.text: Only the polynomial expansion, since it multiplies test values
options.why: Multiplying a row's own values uses nothing from other rows. The scaler's mean does.
A scaler's mean and spread are estimated, like coefficients. Estimating them on test rows lets the test period shape the inputs.

feedback.correct: Anything estimated from rows leaks if test rows are among them.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which transform computes something across rows.

explain.text: The scaler's mean is an average over rows, so test rows shift it. Lesson 9 shows how that flatters a backtest. Fit every transform on training rows, even the harmless ones, so the habit never fails.
